epic.intent:
Dark Mechanicus is Scrum with sub-agents as the developers. Run 1 of the Mechanicus UI revamp showed that the cadence is off: every node gets the full treatment.

**What we saw (sprint 1 of the UI revamp)**
- **No downleveling.** The matcher treats reasoning level only as a floor and never rewards a model that fits. `quality: high` (set by both repo profiles and copied into 11 of 12 tickets) is effectively a bonus for the biggest model, and cost only counts when a ticket asks for it (none do). Opus wrote a docs-only palette proposal. The small model was eligible for four tickets and was never chosen. Every mid-tier pick overrode the score.
- **No size or effort.** Tickets have no size, no "micro" flag and no reasoning effort, and a claim records only the model.
- **Heavy nodes.** After every ticket the orchestrator re-ran all six checks on the integrated branch, took screenshots and made its own merge commit: 19 commits for 7 tickets.
- **Checkpoints read like audits, not sprint reviews.** There is no retro, and nothing turns leftovers or discoveries into the next sprint.

**The cadence we want, mirroring a real Scrum team**
1. **Right-sized developers.** Every ticket has an honest size (micro, small, medium, large) and effort. The orchestrator dispatches the smallest model that fits, at that effort, and escalates one tier at a time only after a rejection.
2. **Light tickets.** A sub-agent does each ticket and runs targeted checks. Review checks that ticket's acceptance criteria from that evidence and nothing more.
3. **Row checks.** When a row of parallel tickets (same-sprint dependency depth) is accepted, the orchestrator checks that the code combined cleanly before more work builds on it.
4. **A planned acceptance round.** Every sprint ends in an acceptance node: one verification step per item, planned up front, plus the project's Definition of Done (full tests, coverage thresholds, fireguard, deadcode, build).
5. **One commit per sprint.** The sprint is squashed into a single commit on the epic branch, and the server verifies it.
6. **Retro.** The sprint report becomes a sprint review and retrospective: what was delivered and how to see it, what went well and poorly, whether each developer was sized right, discoveries, and leftovers.
7. **Redraft.** The retro feeds the next sprint: leftovers move with a fresh retry budget and discoveries become tickets. The person approves the retro and the redraft in one step.

**Out of scope:** running checks on the server (DM still records evidence and does not execute builds), merging the epic into the default branch (still a person's step), and changing the in-flight UI revamp run.

successCriteria.text: For a ticket with no cost or quality preference, match_capabilities recommends the cheapest eligible model whose reasoning range fits the ticket, explains why, and after a rejection recommends one tier (or one effort) up; a deep ticket still matches only deep-capable models.
Every ticket can carry a size (micro, small, medium, large) and a reasoning effort; both show in the ticket view and on graph nodes, and every claim records the model and effort actually used.

Every sprint ends in an acceptance node that runs after all of the sprint's other required tickets, plans one verification step per ticket plus the project's Definition of Done (including code coverage thresholds), and the checkpoint cannot be approved until it is accepted.

Per-ticket review checks acceptance criteria from the worker's targeted evidence only; the full sweep runs once, in the acceptance node; a failed row integration check blocks the tickets that build on that row.
Each sprint lands on the epic branch as exactly one squashed commit, which the server verifies and the sprint report shows.

Every sprint report carries a retro (delivered items with how to see them, went well, went poorly, tier fit per ticket from real attempts, discoveries, leftovers), shown on the checkpoint screen and the completed-epic overview.

At a checkpoint the next sprint is redrafted from the retro (leftovers moved with a fresh retry budget, discoveries added as tickets), the person approves the retro and the redraft in one step, and the run continues on the redrafted plan.

epic.title: Scrum cadence: right-sized agents, a sprint acceptance round, one-commit increments, retro and redraft

bundle.rationale:
**Why three sprints, in this order.** They follow the person's priorities: (1) right-size the developers, (2) make tickets light and move the heavy testing into a planned acceptance round with one commit per sprint, (3) add the retro and the redraft. Sprint 1 cuts cost immediately and is self-contained. Sprint 2 is the riskiest (a new ticket kind, gates, rows, git verification) and lands before the retro, which depends on acceptance nodes and sizes.

**This epic dogfoods the cadence before it exists.** Every ticket is sized (a `size:` tag until DM-24 adds the field), micro tasks are called out (DM-27, DM-30), and capabilities are written by hand at `quality: standard` with `cost: low`, rather than copied from the repo profiles, which force the biggest model today. Only DM-40 is `deep`. Each work ticket's own checks are targeted (the touched tests plus typecheck). Each sprint ends with an acceptance ticket that requires every other ticket in the sprint, plans one verification criterion per item, runs the full sweep once and squashes the sprint into one commit. Until DM-38 lands, acceptance tickets keep a tier-fit table in their evidence notes so each sprint report can carry a hand-written retro.

**Graph.** In sprint 1, DM-24 (schema) comes first; DM-25, DM-26 and DM-27 run in parallel after it; DM-28 follows DM-25. In sprint 2 there are three parallel starts: DM-29 and DM-30 (independent), DM-31 then DM-32 (the acceptance-node chain), and DM-34 (rows). DM-33 joins DM-32 and DM-29; DM-35 follows DM-32; DM-36 joins all of them; DM-37 follows the server tickets. Sprint 3 is a chain: DM-38, DM-39, DM-40, then DM-41 and DM-42. The critical path is DM-31, DM-32, DM-35, DM-36, then acceptance.

**Assumptions to confirm**
1. The squashed sprint commit lands on the **epic branch** (`scrum-cadence`). Merging the epic into the default branch stays a person's step, as today.
2. DM keeps recording evidence and does not run checks. The Definition of Done gate checks named, reported checks. Only the increment is verified independently, with read-only git.
3. Coverage thresholds start at the measured baseline, rounded down, so coverage cannot regress. Raise them later.
4. The size scale is micro, small, medium and large; `large` warns to split.
5. A row is same-sprint dependency depth (the graph's rows), excluding the acceptance node. A row check holds back only the work built on that row; it is not a sprint-wide barrier.
6. New gates (acceptance, Definition of Done, increment, retro) apply only to sprints that have an acceptance node, so in-flight runs on older plans, including the UI revamp, keep working.
7. Skills stay vendor-neutral (enforced by skills.test.ts). The Claude Code specifics go in a host runbook.
8. The orchestrator for this epic runs on the installed app. Sprint 1's matcher and skills only take effect for later sprints after the app is rebuilt and installed.

acceptanceCriteria.text: create_ticket, update_ticket and update_plan_draft accept `size` and `capability.reasoning.effort`; get_ticket and list_tickets return them; changing either shows up in the draft's changes.
A plan snapshot and a run history saved before this change (use ones from `.darkmechanicus/` as fixtures) still import, parse and keep their content hash.
validate_plan warns, without erroring, on a `large` ticket and on a `micro` ticket at `deep`.
register_host accepts per-model `efforts`; claim_ticket records `worker.effort`, refuses an effort the model does not declare, and the execution packet and exported run history carry it.
The new tests were written first and failed for the right reason before the change; the touched test files and typecheck pass.

tickets.body:
Size: **medium**. Today a ticket has no size and no effort. The only intensity signal is `reasoning.level` (`routine`, `multi_step`, `deep`), which is a floor, not a fit. Add both, so planners can call out micro tasks and the orchestrator can dispatch at a matching model and effort.

**Ticket size.** Add an optional `size` on the ticket: `micro`, `small`, `medium` or `large`.
- micro: one obvious change in one or two files, one targeted test, no design choice.
- small: one coherent change inside one module.
- medium: several modules, or one real design choice.
- large: should usually be split.

**Reasoning effort.** Add an optional `capability.reasoning.effort`: `low`, `medium` or `high`. It is provider-neutral (how hard the worker should think), separate from `level` (what the model must be capable of).

**Host catalog and claims.**
- `register_host` models gain optional `efforts`: the efforts the host can run that model at.
- The `claim_ticket` `worker` gains optional `effort`. Refuse an effort the model does not declare, when it declares any. Record the effort on the attempt (`WorkerInfo`), return it in the execution packet, and export it in run history.

**Validation warnings** (not errors): a `large` ticket (suggest splitting); a `micro` ticket at `deep`.

**Compatibility (must hold).** `planBundle` and `capabilityProfile` are strict objects, and portable snapshots are checked against their content hash (`src/core/repo/portable.ts:114-119`). The new fields are optional and get **no** zod `.default()`, so plans saved before this change still parse and keep their hash. Keep `PLAN_FORMAT_VERSION` unless a migration is truly needed.

**Where**
- Capability schema: `src/core/schemas.ts:75-109`. Host catalog schema: `src/core/schemas.ts:297-317`.
- `src/shared/domain/bundle.ts:45-77,184-206` and `src/core/plan/normalize.ts:66-84`.
- `src/core/plan/diff.ts`: size and effort edits show as draft changes.
- `src/core/plan/graph.ts`: the `validatePlan` warnings.
- `src/core/commandSchemas.ts:105-118`: the claim worker.
- `src/shared/domain/views.ts:208-215,290-308`.
- `src/core/services/attempts.ts:172-190,223-247`.
- The portable attempt schema in `src/core/repo/portable.ts`.
- The MCP tool descriptions for `create_ticket`, `update_ticket`, `update_plan_draft`, `register_host` and `claim_ticket`.

**Checks for this ticket:** targeted only, meaning the tests for the files you touch plus `npm run typecheck`. The full sweep runs in the sprint acceptance ticket.

reasoning.rationale: Schema change across core, MCP and portable records under a strict snapshot-hash compatibility constraint.

acceptanceCriteria.text: With a fixture catalog shaped like the live one (a deep model at high cost, a multi_step model at normal cost, a routine model at low cost), a routine ticket with no preferences recommends the routine model, a multi_step ticket the multi_step model, and a deep ticket only the deep model.
`quality: high` on a routine or multi_step ticket does not put a deeper model first, and a model listing more skill tags does not beat a better-fitting model on tags alone.
Equal scores sort by cost tier, cheaper first, then by model id.
The result includes `recommended` with model, effort and reasons; after a rejected attempt it recommends one tier up, or a higher effort on the same model when no tier is above.
`reasons` explains the fit, cost and quality terms; the tests were written first and failed before the change; the touched tests and typecheck pass.

tickets.body:
Size: **small**. The matcher never steers work to a cheaper model. In run 1 of the UI revamp, Opus wrote a docs-only palette proposal, and the small model, though eligible on four tickets, was never picked. Every mid-tier pick overrode the score.

**Why** (all in `src/core/plan/capabilities.ts`)
- Reasoning is only a floor (`:59-70`). `scoreModel` (`:107-116`) never compares the model's highest level with the ticket's, so an over-capable model loses nothing.
- `quality: high` gives +15 only to deep-capable models (`:24-27`), even on routine tickets. Both repo profiles set it.
- Cost tiers count only when `cost: low` (`:28-37`), and nothing sets that.
- Each skill tag the model self-declares adds +10 (`:108-109`). The host declared 10 tags for its biggest model and 1 for its smallest.
- Ties sort by model id (`:133`).

**Change**
1. **Fit.** Penalise each reasoning rank by which a model's highest level exceeds the ticket's need (use `REASONING_RANK`, `rankOf` and `highestLevel` at `:14,45-57`), and say so in `reasons`.
2. **Quality.** `quality: high` must not put a deeper model ahead of one that fits. It may break ties among fitting models.
3. **Cost.** With no cost preference, a cheaper `costTier` beats a pricier one at equal fit. Ties sort by cost tier, then by id.
4. **Skills.** Tag matches cannot outweigh fit: cap them, or count only the tags the ticket needs.
5. **Size.** `micro` and `small` tickets (from the size ticket in this sprint) favour the cheapest fitting model.
6. **Recommendation.** Add `recommended { modelId, effort, reasons }` to the result: the top fit, at the ticket's effort or, when that is unset, `low` for micro and small, `medium` for medium and `high` for large.
7. **Escalation.** After a rejected or failed attempt on the ticket in this run, recommend the cheapest eligible model one tier above the last attempt's model. When nothing is above it, recommend the same model at a higher effort. This needs the run's attempts (`matchCapabilities` in `src/core/services/hosts.ts:52-60`).

The hard filters stay as they are: a deep ticket still matches only deep-capable models.

**Checks for this ticket:** the targeted tests for `capabilities.ts` and `hosts.ts`, plus typecheck.

reasoning.rationale: A small scoring module, but the fit, cost and escalation rules need careful cases.

tickets.body:
Size: **small**. Nothing in the skills pushes toward cheaper workers. `skills/planner.md:44-49` lists the reasoning levels with no guidance on when to pick `routine`, and tells planners to start from a profile, which copied `quality: high`. `skills/orchestrator.md:30-34` says to choose by score and judgment.

**planner.md**
- A sizing rubric: micro, small, medium and large, with one example each.
- Call out micro tasks explicitly, and set an effort.
- Leave `quality` unset unless the person asked for it.
- Split `large` tickets.
- Say that precise ticket bodies are what let small workers succeed.

**orchestrator.md**
- Register each model's efforts.
- Take `recommended` from match_capabilities unless there is a stated reason not to, and dispatch at the recommended effort.
- On a rejection, escalate one tier (or one effort step), never straight to the top, and put the reason in the claim `rationale`.
- Report repeated escalations as profile proposals.

**docs/runbooks**
- Add a Claude Code host runbook. Vendor names are fine in docs, not in skills.
- Give an example catalog for the current model family, with cost tiers and efforts.
- Show how to dispatch a subagent at a given model and effort. Agent definitions under `.claude/agents/` carry the model and effort; verify how effort is actually set before documenting it.

**Constraints**
- Keep the skills vendor-neutral (`src/mcp/skills.test.ts:14,48-49`) and update the required phrases there.
- Bump `SKILLS_VERSION` in `src/core/version.ts:2`.

**Checks for this ticket:** `src/mcp/skills.test.ts` and typecheck.

acceptanceCriteria.text: A ticket can be created with kind acceptance; add_sprint and create_epic create one per new sprint; a second acceptance node in a sprint is a validation error.
validate_plan warns for a sprint with work tickets but no acceptance node, and for each required work ticket that no acceptance criterion covers.
An edge from the acceptance node to a ticket in its own sprint is rejected, and moving the node to another sprint is refused.
Plans and snapshots saved before this change parse, keep their hash, and validate with warnings only.
The tests were written first; the touched tests and typecheck pass.

tickets.body:
Size: **medium**. The full verification sweep should be a planned node at the end of every sprint, not repeated on every ticket. This ticket adds the node to plans. The next ticket gates the run on it.

- **Kind.** Add a ticket `kind`: `work` (absent means work) or `acceptance`. It is optional, with no zod default, for the same snapshot-hash reason as size and effort.
- **One per sprint.** A second acceptance node in a sprint is a validation error. A sprint with work tickets but no acceptance node is a validation warning, so older plans still save.
- **Created automatically.** `add_sprint` and `create_epic` create the sprint's acceptance node (title "Sprint N acceptance", workType `testing`, criteria to fill in). The desktop will offer to add one to a sprint that lacks it: the renderer work comes in the UI ticket, but the op must exist here.
- **Implicit dependencies.** The acceptance node implicitly requires every other required ticket in its sprint. No edges are stored, so moving tickets between sprints needs no rewiring.
  - An explicit edge into it from its own sprint is redundant and gets a warning.
  - An edge out of it to a ticket in its own sprint is an error, because it runs last.
  - Later sprints may depend on it.
  - It cannot be moved to another sprint.
- **Per-item coverage.** An acceptance criterion may carry `covers: <ticketId>`. Validation warns for each required work ticket in the sprint that no criterion covers, so the planner plans a verification step per item.
- Views, diffs and portable records carry `kind` and `covers`.

**Where**
- `src/core/schemas.ts` (ticket, criterion) and `src/shared/domain/bundle.ts`.
- `src/core/plan/draftOps.ts:95-176`.
- `src/core/plan/graph.ts` (`validatePlan` at `:325`).
- `src/core/plan/normalize.ts` and `src/core/plan/diff.ts`.
- `src/core/repo/portable.ts`.
- The MCP tool descriptions.

**Checks for this ticket:** the targeted tests for the touched plan modules, plus typecheck.

reasoning.rationale: New ticket kind with implicit edges, validation and draft-op rules, under the snapshot compatibility constraint.

Size: **medium**. Make the acceptance node the sprint's last step in execution.

- **Readiness.** An acceptance node is ready only when every other required ticket in its sprint is accepted. Until then `get_ready_tickets` lists it as blocked, with those tickets as prerequisites (`src/core/plan/readiness.ts:145-170`).
- **New gate `acceptance_accepted`.** It requires an accepted, non-superseded attempt on the sprint's acceptance node (`src/core/services/checkpoints.ts:164-173`, and `GateConditionId` in `src/shared/domain/views.ts:354-360`). Sprints without an acceptance node (older plans) don't get the gate.
- `get_run` shows acceptance nodes with their implicit prerequisites.
- Update the `get_checkpoint` description (`src/mcp/tools/checkpoints.ts:28`).

The checkpoint screen loops over conditions, so the gate appears without renderer work.

**Checks for this ticket:** the targeted tests for readiness and checkpoints, plus typecheck. Add one integration test that runs a two-ticket sprint with an acceptance node through to the checkpoint.

reasoning.rationale: Readiness and gate changes that must leave older plans untouched.

acceptanceCriteria.text: get_project returns the Definition of Done; set_definition_of_done changes it for planner and desktop sessions and is refused for workers.
The acceptance node's execution packet lists the Definition of Done checks.
The checkpoint shows definition_of_done unmet until the accepted acceptance attempt reports every named check as passed, and names the missing ones.
This repository's project config holds the seven checks with their commands.
The tests were written first; the touched tests and typecheck pass.

tickets.body:
Size: **medium**. In Scrum the Definition of Done belongs to the team, not to one story. Store it once per project and make every sprint's acceptance node prove it.

- **Project-level `definitionOfDone`.** Ordered checks, each `{ name, command, description }`.
  - Stored in `.darkmechanicus/project.json`, so it is portable and travels with the repo.
  - Returned by `get_project`.
  - Set by a new `set_definition_of_done` for planner and desktop sessions. Add a new capability following the patterns in `src/core/authz.ts`.
- **New gate `definition_of_done`** on sprints with an acceptance node: the node's accepted attempt has a `passed` check in its evidence for every DoD name. DM still doesn't run commands; it checks the named evidence.
- The acceptance node's execution packet includes the DoD, so the worker knows what to run.
- **Seed this repository's DoD:** lint, typecheck, test, coverage, fireguard (base = the sprint's start commit), deadcode and build, each with its npm command.

**Checks for this ticket:** the targeted tests for project config, authz and checkpoints, plus typecheck.

reasoning.rationale: New portable project setting, a capability and a gate that reads attempt evidence.

tickets.title: Record the project's Definition of Done and require it in the acceptance node

get_ready_tickets and get_run report each ticket's row and each row's latest check.
record_row_check stores a row check; while a row's latest check has failed, its dependents and the acceptance node show row_check_failed, and a passing check clears it.
Row checks are exported with the run history and survive a re-import.

tickets.body:
Size: **medium**. The orchestrator should check that a row of parallel work combined cleanly before more work builds on it. Rows exist only in the renderer today (`src/renderer/src/graph/graphModel.ts:255-287`, `sprintDepths` and `groupByDepth`), and the server has no layer concept (`docs/architecture.md:96`).

- **Rows in core.** Move the same-sprint dependency depth into core (`src/core/plan/graph.ts`) as the definition of a row: row 1 has no same-sprint prerequisites, and the acceptance node is in no row.
  - The graph renderer uses the shared function, with no visual change.
  - Its 6-column visual wrap stays a rendering detail.

tickets.body:
Size: **medium**. Each sprint should reach the epic branch as one squashed commit, and the server should check that rather than trust it. The git adapter is read-only today and has no ancestry query (`src/core/repo/types.ts:35-45`, `src/core/repo/git.ts:145-163`).

- Add read-only git queries: is-ancestor, and a commit's parents.
- The acceptance node's submission names the sprint increment `{ branch, commit }`.
- **On submit, verify and store the result.**
  - The commit exists and has exactly one parent (it is not a merge).
  - It is reachable from the epic branch.
  - It is not reachable from the previous sprint's increment; for sprint 1, it comes after the epic's start commit.
  - No commit recorded by the sprint's accepted work attempts is reachable from the epic branch. This proves the sprint was squashed, not merged.
- **New gate `increment_merged`** on sprints with an acceptance node. It reads the stored result, because gate evaluation is synchronous SQL; verify at submit time instead.
- Store each sprint's increment on the run. The sprint report and the run history show it.
- The integration target is the epic branch. Merging the epic into the default branch stays a person's step.

**Checks for this ticket:** targeted tests against a temporary git repository, plus typecheck.

reasoning.rationale: Read-only git queries, an async verification stored for a synchronous gate, and squash-versus-merge edge cases.

tickets.body:
Size: **medium**. A checkpoint should read like a sprint review and retrospective: what was delivered and how to see it, what went well and poorly, whether the developers were sized right, what was discovered, and what is left.

**Report input gains an optional `retro`**
- `delivered[]`: `{ ticket, demo, evidence }`, meaning what to look at and where (an artifact, a screenshot or a commit).
- `wentWell[]`, `wentPoorly[]` and `actions[]` (process changes for the next sprint).
- `discoveries[]`: `{ title, body, ticket? }`, for new work found during the sprint.
- `leftovers[]`: `{ ticket, reason }`, for required work that was not accepted.
- `tierFit[]`: `{ ticket, verdict: right_sized | oversized | undersized, note }`.

**Computed tier facts.** The report view adds facts per ticket, computed by the server from attempts rather than written by the reporter: size, planned level and effort, each attempt's model and effort, attempt and rejection counts, and whether it escalated.

**Retro gate.** On sprints with an acceptance node, a report without a retro leaves a new `retro` gate unmet. Older plans are unaffected.

**Compatibility**
- Legacy rows read with `retro: null` (`src/core/services/reports.ts:75-86,103-116`).
- The portable report schema is strict, so it needs `.nullable().default(null)` (`src/core/repo/portable.ts:181-197`).
- Search indexes the retro text (`reports.ts:175-185`, `importer.ts:861-872`).

**Checks for this ticket:** the targeted tests for reports, portable and importer, plus typecheck.

reasoning.rationale: Report schema and storage changes, computed facts from attempts, and strict portable records.

tickets.body:
Size: **medium**. Today follow-ups reach the plan only through the desktop's "+ Add to draft", which carries a title and body only (`src/renderer/src/checkpoint/gateView.ts:233-247`), and leftovers have no path at all. Make the retro drive the next sprint's draft.

**New command `redraft_next_sprint { runId }`** for orchestrator and desktop sessions, at a checkpoint. It opens the epic draft and:
- moves each retro leftover from the active sprint to the next sprint, adding a sprint after the active one if it is the final sprint, and keeps prerequisites valid (moving dependents along when needed);
- adds each discovery as a ticket in the next sprint (title, body, and the source ticket in references), unsized, so the planner must size it;
- returns the draft changes.

The orchestrator then refines the draft with `update_plan_draft`; it already has draft.edit.

**Fresh retry budget.** When a revision is adopted, the failed, rejected and abandoned attempts of a ticket that moved to a later sprint are superseded, so a leftover doesn't arrive already at its retry limit (`src/core/services/adoption.ts:85-106`, `src/core/plan/readiness.ts:126-143`).

**Run-aware draft warnings.** While a run is active, editing a sprint the run has already passed, or inserting a sprint before the active one, is a validation warning.

**Checks for this ticket:** the targeted tests for the command, adoption and readiness, plus typecheck.

reasoning.rationale: A draft-building command plus changes to adoption and readiness that touch retry accounting.
